c.tagline: Mediterranean port city cascading down Mount Carmel to the golden-domed Bahá'í Gardens.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis (monit) are legally required to run the meter (moneh); insist on it, especially from the airport or train station, since some drivers may push for a flat rate instead.

emergency.note: 102 reaches fire and rescue services; 100 and 101 are the most commonly used emergency numbers in daily life.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Safe; follow local security guidance given regional tensions

hood_desc: A restored 19th-century Templer colony of stone houses turned into cafes, restaurants and galleries, running straight up to the foot of the Bahá'í Gardens; best for first-time visitors who want the signature view and easy dining.
A historic Arab-Christian neighborhood known for its market, murals and mixed Jewish-Arab street life; suits travelers wanting an authentic, less touristy feel and some of the city's best hummus.
A dense commercial district partway up the mountain with the Carmelit funicular's lower stations, markets and budget shopping; central and convenient though less polished than the areas above it.
The upscale plateau atop Mount Carmel with panoramic promenades, business hotels and the university nearby; suits travelers wanting views, quieter streets and higher-end lodging.
A seafront strip near the beach, the cable car up to Stella Maris and Rambam hospital; good for travelers wanting beach access and a quieter, more local feel.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: Buses and the Carmelit generally run from around 5:30 AM to midnight on weekdays; nearly all public transport, including the Carmelit, shuts down from Friday afternoon until Saturday evening for Shabbat.
transit.pay: Pay with a rechargeable Rav-Kav smart card (available at kiosks and stations) or through the Moovit app; cash fares are also accepted on board buses.
transit.note: Haifa is the only Israeli city with an underground rail system, the six-station Carmelit funicular linking downtown to Mount Carmel; it's the oldest underground transit system in the Middle East.

air: Ben Gurion Airport (TLV), near Tel Aviv
Haifa Airport (HFA) - limited regional flights to Athens and Larnaca
train: Israel Railways coastal line (Haifa–Tel Aviv–Ben Gurion Airport)
Israel Railways Jezreel Valley line (Haifa–Beit She'an via Afula)
bus: Egged and Nateev Express city/regional buses

transit.m: Israel Railways direct train, Ben Gurion Airport–Haifa (~55-70 min)
Nateev Express intercity bus or shared taxi (sherut)

tip.r: Around 12% is standard at restaurants and is sometimes added automatically for larger groups; tipping taxi drivers isn't required but rounding up is common.

food.name: Hummus
food.desc: Warm, loose hummus finished with whole chickpeas, ful or tahini, eaten for breakfast with raw onion, pickles and hot pita straight from the oven.

places.name: Hummus Abu Marwan
places.note: Long-running port hummusiya, packed with dockworkers and locals from mid-morning.

places.name: Abu Yousef
places.note: Family hummus house running since the 1930s, one of the oldest in the country.

places.name: Ein El Wadi
places.note: Neighbourhood kitchen serving hummus alongside home-style Arab dishes.

food.name: Falafel
food.desc: Herb-green chickpea fritters fried to order and stuffed into pita with salad, tahini, pickles and chips; a Wadi Nisnas street-corner ritual.

places.name: Falafel HaZkenim
places.note: The city's best-known falafel counter, running for decades on the same corner.

places.name: Falafel Michel
places.note: Local rival to HaZkenim with a devoted following; fried fresh in small batches.

places.name: Falafel HaNasi
places.note: Uphill option handy for visitors staying near the Baha'i Gardens.

food.name: Wadi Nisnas mezze
food.desc: Arab home cooking spread across the table: labneh, muhammara, stuffed vine leaves, maqluba and slow-cooked lamb with rice and toasted nuts.

places.name: Fattoush
places.note: Landmark Arab restaurant with a garden terrace under the Baha'i Gardens.

places.name: Douzan
places.note: Arab-French kitchen that helped define Haifa's mixed-city dining scene.

places.name: Ein El Wadi
places.note: Small, unfussy dining room in the market alleys cooking daily home-style specials.

food.name: Grilled Mediterranean fish
food.desc: Whole denis or locus grilled over coals with lemon, tahini and a wall of salads, plus fried calamari and shrimp from the boats below the city.

places.name: Jacko Street Fish
places.note: Veteran seafood restaurant near the port, a Haifa fixture for grilled whole fish.

places.name: Fattoush
places.note: Reliable grilled fish alongside its mezze, with the best terrace in the city.

places.name: Downtown port fish houses
places.note: Cluster of simple fish restaurants near the old customs house, cheaper than the Colony.

food.name: Druze pita with labneh and zaatar
food.desc: Paper-thin saj bread baked on a domed griddle and rolled around labneh, olive oil and zaatar; made in the Druze villages on the Carmel ridge.

places.name: Daliyat al-Karmel village market
places.note: Main-street bakeries and stalls make saj bread to order all day.

places.name: Isfiya village eateries
places.note: Quieter Druze village next door with family kitchens serving the same breads.

places.name: Talpiot Market stalls
places.note: City market where Druze bakers sell saj bread and labneh without the drive uphill.

food.name: Knafeh Nabulsiyeh
food.desc: Shredded pastry over stretchy white cheese, baked orange, drenched in rose-scented syrup and scattered with crushed pistachio; sold by the tray.

places.name: Wadi Nisnas sweet shops
places.note: Several sweet shops along the market alley cut knafeh fresh from hot trays.

places.name: Douzan
places.note: Sit-down version of the classic with coffee, on the main boulevard.

places.name: Talpiot Market
places.note: Market bakeries sell knafeh and baklava by weight, cheaper than the tourist strip.

food.name: Arabic coffee
food.desc: Dark coffee boiled with cardamom and poured into small cups, sold beside sacks of freshly roasted beans and spices in the market lanes.

places.name: Wadi Nisnas coffee roasters
places.note: Roasteries grind cardamom into the beans on the spot; the neighbourhood smells of it.

places.name: Fattoush
places.note: Garden tables for a slow cup after mezze, open late.

places.name: Talpiot Market
places.note: Market coffee stands serving traders and shoppers from early morning.

food.name: Arak
food.desc: Aniseed spirit poured over ice and clouded with water, drunk slowly through a mezze meal; the standard table drink across the mixed city.

places.name: Maayan Habira
places.note: Historic drinking house from the Romanian-Jewish era, now a beloved bar and kitchen.

places.name: Douzan
places.note: Bar-restaurant on the boulevard where arak and mezze run late into the night.

places.name: Fattoush
places.note: Terrace bar under the gardens, a classic spot for arak with grilled dishes.

landmarks: Bahá'í Gardens and Shrine of the Báb
Nineteen immaculate garden terraces cascade a kilometer down Mount Carmel to a golden-domed shrine, a UNESCO World Heritage marvel and Haifa's defining panorama.
German Colony (Ben Gurion Boulevard)
Restored 19th-century Templer houses now host cafés and restaurants along this palm-lined boulevard, perfectly aligned beneath the illuminated Bahá'í terraces.
Stella Maris Carmelite Monastery
Perched on Mount Carmel's seaward cliff above Elijah's grotto, this 19th-century monastery pairs an ornate painted dome with sweeping Mediterranean views.
Louis Promenade (Yefe Nof)
This flower-edged clifftop walkway atop Mount Carmel unfurls Haifa's signature vista over the Bahá'í gardens, the port and the sweep of Haifa Bay toward Lebanon.
Cave of Elijah
Venerated by Jews, Christians, Muslims and Druze alike, this grotto at Mount Carmel's foot is revered as the prophet Elijah's shelter and place of prayer.
Wadi Nisnas
Haifa's Arab quarter buzzes with a fragrant market, legendary falafel stands and open-air artworks celebrating the city's tradition of Jewish-Arab coexistence.
Madatech (Israel National Museum of Science)
Housed in the historic Technion building where Einstein once planted a palm tree, this hands-on science museum delights families amid landmark 1912 architecture.
Tikotin Museum of Japanese Art
The only museum in the Middle East devoted to Japanese art displays exquisite prints, ceramics and samurai artifacts in a serene Carmel hilltop setting.
Bat Galim Promenade
Haifa's breezy seafront neighborhood offers a wave-splashed boardwalk, surfers and the cable car ascending to Stella Maris, ideal for a sunset stroll.
Haifa Port and Downtown (Turkish Market quarter)
The revitalized lower city mixes Ottoman-era lanes, hip bars and galleries beneath cranes of the historic port, Haifa's gritty-turned-trendy nightlife district.

train.note: Haifa is the best-served rail city in Israel outside Tel Aviv, with four stations - Hof HaCarmel in the south, Bat Galim, Haifa Center HaShmona by the port and Lev HaMifratz in the bay - and three to four trains an hour to Tel Aviv at peak, taking a little over an hour. Direct services also run to Ben Gurion Airport, Akko, Nahariya, Beer Sheva and inland to Beit She'an. Everything stops from Friday afternoon until Saturday night for Shabbat, so plan around it. There are no international trains: the historic lines to Lebanon and to Damascus through the Jezreel Valley have been closed for decades and those borders are shut.

bus.note: Intercity coaches use two hubs, both built on top of train stations - Merkazit Hof HaCarmel in the south for Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, and Merkazit HaMifratz in the bay for the north and east. Egged (https://www.egged.co.il/) runs line 910 from Tel Aviv, 940 and 960 from Jerusalem and 947 from Ben Gurion Airport, while Nateev Express (https://www.nateevexpress.com/) covers much of the Galilee. Fares are paid with a Rav-Kav card or app rather than cash on most routes, and nothing runs on Shabbat. No coach goes abroad from Haifa: for Jordan you take a bus to Beit She'an, cross at the Sheikh Hussein/Jordan River bridge and continue by Jordanian taxi or bus.

intl.to: Akko (Israel) - small foot-passenger boat across Haifa Bay from Gate 5 at the port
intl.op: local operator, tickets at the quay (seasonal, no online booking)

ferry.note: The Port of Haifa has a modern passenger terminal and handled around a quarter of a million cruise passengers in 2018, but there is no longer any scheduled international ferry - the old Haifa-Limassol-Piraeus sailings ended in the 2000s and have not returned. The only regular passenger boat is the little foot ferry across the bay to Akko, which runs a couple of times a day midweek and more often on Saturdays and makes an easy day trip in either direction. It is weather-dependent and effectively a warm-season service. For a sea crossing to Cyprus, Greece or Turkey you would have to fly out and pick up a ferry elsewhere in the eastern Mediterranean.

half.name: Akko (Acre)
half.blurb: Walled Crusader port city with underground tunnels, a hospitaller fortress, and an active Ottoman-era market.

half.name: Caesarea
half.blurb: Roman port city ruins with a restored amphitheater, hippodrome, and Crusader-era harbor walls on the Mediterranean coast.

half.name: Nazareth
half.blurb: Jesus's childhood town, with the Basilica of the Annunciation and a historic market in the old city.

half.name: Rosh HaNikra
half.blurb: Chalk sea grottoes at the Lebanon border reached by cable car, carved by wave erosion into white cliffs.

half.name: Zichron Ya'akov
half.blurb: Wine-country hilltop town founded by Baron Rothschild, with a preserved 19th-century main street and boutique wineries.
